source_read: PDF, pp. 1–8 (published version, Journal of Forensic and Legal Medicine 122 (2026) 103200, printed page numbers used; all pages; text extracted with pdftotext -layout; pp. 1–6 checked on 150-dpi renders). Supplementary material (PRISMA flow diagram, Supplementary Table 1) not read. Only the parts of the claim that rest on this source were judged; the Strömmer et al. (2020) parts were not checked here.

claims.overstatement: The parts attributed to this review are accurate and hedged ('without figures', 'second-hand'). Three points. (1) Both directions: on whether the state kills without restraint, the review also reports, from case reports, that deaths attributed to ExDS may occur without overt restraint or first look like homicide (p. 4, section 3.5, 4th paragraph, refs 57–58). The claim gives only the pooled analysis's 'no evidence' reading and the editors' critique of it, so for balance it should add this second-hand statement; the claim's 'evidence is insufficient' framing stays right. (2) 'The authors of both reviews ... reject the term' is slightly strong for this review: the authors favour 'acute behavioral disturbance', keep 'ExD' when citing the literature (p. 1, Introduction, 3rd paragraph), and recommend replacing it 'where possible' and using it cautiously (p. 5, section 5, 6th paragraph). (3) 'Mainly in medico-legal reports of deaths' is fair for this review's account of use in death investigation (abstract; p. 2), but the review also describes a 10-feature ExD checklist used in police and prehospital practice, with features recorded in a minority of use-of-force encounters with living people (p. 3, section 3.1, 3rd paragraph).
claims.note: Numbers from this source checked on the renders: search 1 January 2010 to 1 September 2025 (English or Portuguese, PubMed and Scopus); Finland 12 of 21,036 autopsies (0.06%; recomputed 0.057%); 229 deaths, 58% within 1–5 minutes of starting prone restraint, verbal respiratory distress in at least 20% before collapse; Ontario 46 investigative reports, most classified accidental or natural; 116 included studies, 62 good (53.4%), 51 fair (44.0%), 3 weak (2.6%), recomputed. Context the magnitude could carry: the 229 deaths are cited to refs 24 and 29, and ref 24 is titled as a study of civil-litigated prone-restraint deaths (p. 7), so that series is selected through litigation; the Ontario series (ref 14) is a socio-legal analysis of coroners' material in a social-justice journal, and the Introduction uses the same source for critics' view that restraint deaths are classed as accidental or natural (p. 2); the statement that cocaine, methamphetamine and phencyclidine are 'frequently identified' rests on a 2012 defining review and a 2009 book chapter (refs 11, 38). The only drug-adjacent proportion in the review is TASER judged contributory in 27% of 75 deaths temporally associated with TASER (p. 3), which is not a count of drug involvement, so 'no counts of drug involvement' stands. The review calls a pooled case analysis and a philosophy-of-science paper narrative reviews that converge on a multifactorial explanation (p. 4, refs 32 and 65).

anchors.extracted: Systematic search of PubMed and Scopus (2010–2025) under PRISMA 2009; deaths in custody described as predominantly multifactorial (restraint, physiological stress, intoxication with psychoactive substances, obesity or cardiac disease); 'excited delirium' highly controversial, without validated diagnostic criteria or specific biomarkers, frequently used as a diagnosis of exclusion in medico-legal contexts; prolonged prone restraint with thoracic or cervical compression may precipitate metabolic acidosis and restraint-associated cardiac arrest even without significant hypoxaemia.

Authors favour 'Acute Behavioral Disturbance' (ABD) as the primary term; 'excited delirium' described as controversial and lacking formal diagnostic validation; ExD kept only when referring to historical concepts, search strategies or the terminology of the original studies.

ExD lacks validated and consensual diagnostic criteria; the controversy goes beyond the lack of validated criteria in official classifications such as the DSM or ICD; the term is frequently invoked in medico-legal contexts to explain in-custody deaths, raising concerns of racial bias and of deflecting responsibility from dangerous restraint; critics see it as racializing and as shifting scrutiny from police violence to the individual; restraint deaths are frequently classified as accidental or natural (ref 14).

PRISMA 2009, narrative synthesis (no meta-analysis); a predefined thematic subset of a broader review; PubMed and Scopus, 1 January 2010 to 1 September 2025, English or Portuguese; earlier 'frequently cited or foundational' studies admitted; two articles added during peer review; two independent screeners. 116 included studies rated 62 good (53.4%), 51 fair (44.0%), 3 weak (2.6%).

Arrest-related deaths involving prone restraint predominantly in young or middle-aged males, often with obesity and psychostimulant intoxication, commonly with handcuffing and body weight on the torso; no counts.

Prospective controlled studies occasionally report low mortality; Finland: 12 restraint-associated deaths among 21,036 autopsies (0.06%) (ref 7); a retrospective review of 229 deaths: 58% within 1–5 minutes of starting prone restraint, verbal respiratory distress documented in at least 20% before cardiac collapse (refs 24, 29; ref 24 titled as a study of civil-litigated cases); persistent under-reporting in official vital statistics asserted from ref 29, without figures.

ExD features documented in a minority of use-of-force encounters, their accumulation associated with hyperthermia; a 10-feature behavioural and physiological checklist used in law-enforcement and prehospital literature; features most often in young men, frequently under psychostimulants such as cocaine or methamphetamine, or with psychiatric illness; racialized minorities over-represented among deaths classified as 'legal intervention'.

Two models: current evidence said to strongly favour ventilatory compromise with metabolic collapse (prone restraint cardiac arrest), terminal rhythms mostly PEA or asystole; the stress-induced arrhythmic model (catecholamine surge, stimulant intoxication, subclinical heart disease) described as increasingly challenged because ventricular arrhythmias are absent in most restraint deaths.

Cocaine, methamphetamine and phencyclidine 'frequently identified in toxicological analyses' (refs 11, 38), no proportions, specimens or concentrations; no pathognomonic autopsy findings, so ExDS treated as a diagnosis of exclusion (refs 41–44).

An analysis of 46 investigative reports in Ontario: frequent interplay between restraint and individual risk factors such as substance use or comorbidities; most deaths classified as accidental or natural (ref 14).
Atypical presentations and scene reconstructions show that deaths attributed to ExDS may occur without overt restraint or may at first resemble homicide (refs 57, 58, case reports).

HSP70 expression found in people with documented cocaine use whatever the ExD diagnosis, so read as a non-specific stress response; post-mortem data limited and anatomically restricted; comprehensive toxicology indispensable to distinguish intoxication from other mechanisms in deaths first attributed to ExD.

ExD applied inconsistently, no validated criteria, overlaps with intoxication, agitation and other acute conditions, no specific biomarkers; sympathetic and HPA activation may trigger malignant arrhythmias, especially with intense stress and stimulant intoxication; what the review calls narrative reviews (refs 32 and 65) said to converge on combined effects of psychoactive substances, resistance to restraint, hyperthermia, high-risk positioning and physiological stress rather than a distinct entity.

Catecholaminergic surge allowed as a potential terminal pathway in some custodial deaths, particularly with stimulant intoxication; no single pathological or molecular finding establishes causality. Recommendation: continued use of ExD to be approached with caution and replaced where possible by ABD.

Two databases; publication bias possible; heterogeneity; evidence mostly from high-income countries; primary literature overwhelmingly observational and retrospective, relying on autopsy summaries, police use-of-force logs and civil-litigation records without standardized clinical variables; ties between some death-investigation systems and law enforcement may bias causal interpretation and reporting.

reporting_issues.note: 68 references; methods references 15–22 = 8; book chapters/textbooks (6, 12, 38, 68), a commentary (13) and a philosophy-of-science paper (65) among the rest.
The 'systematic evaluation' sentence on p. 3 carries no citation; ref 36 is single-author (Steinberg 2021).
Refs 32 (pooled analysis) and 65 (philosophy of science) checked; the clause about the pooled analysis's published critiques cannot be checked from this PDF.

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low (provisional on item 8) follows from items 2, 4, 7 and 13. The mechanistic preference resting on reviews sharing one author is borne out by the reference list (refs 24, 29, 35, 36 all include Steinberg).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the strong preference for one mechanism and the claim of a solid methodological foundation go beyond a narrative, uncounted synthesis; the p. 3 against p. 4 ventilatory characterisations conflict.

missed: Section 3.1, 3rd paragraph (p. 3): the review describes a 10-feature ExD checklist used in law-enforcement and prehospital practice, with ExD features recorded in a minority of use-of-force encounters with living people (ref 30) and their accumulation associated with hyperthermia; the label is thus used outside death investigation, which qualifies 'applied mainly in medico-legal reports of deaths'. Card KF4 cites this paragraph only for the over-representation of racialized minorities.

Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 1) and section 5, 6th paragraph (p. 5): the authors keep 'ExD' when citing the literature and recommend replacing it 'where possible'; KF2 and KF13 carry the substance, but a claim saying the authors 'reject' the term overstates them slightly.
